extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; general readers interested in the historical development of the press
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of the rise and development of newspapers and the press in colonial America, including key figures (e.g., Franklin, Zenger), institutional changes, regional differences, and the press's role in democracy and nation‑building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of the Press (Zenger trial precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Zenger trial was the forerunner of the great struggle for a free press; it represented an important legal and cultural precedent for press liberty in the colonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a pivotal battle for a free press that influenced later revolutionary sentiment; the text notes the trial's authoritative standing (Gouverneur Morris) and its continuity with earlier fights by printers such as Benjamin Harris and James Franklin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as a new 'Fourth Estate' (political power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism developed into a veritable new Estate — a power hitherto unknown, which Burke said could be more powerful than Lords Spiritual, Lords Temporal, and Commons combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book frames history thereafter as largely the story of this power and those wielding it; born amid adversity, the press became a central political actor shaping national history rather than merely recording events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development of journalism in connection with democracy and nationality
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism grew closely connected with the idea of democracy and contributed materially to the growth of national feeling and unity among the colonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press activity fed and was fed by democratic impulses; the text claims the press contributed to civilization and democratic development 'as no other single factor... except Christianity.' Examples include the press' role in promoting intercolonial correspondence and national sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press's prime office: collection and circulation of intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary function of journalism is to collect and circulate intelligence that enables public opinion in one community to act upon other communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dissemination role is cited as central to building public consciousness and unity (e.g., enabling reaction to the Stamp Act, spreading Franklin's ideas such as 'Join or Die'). The text uses this as an explanatory principle for the press's political influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence and avoidance of 'published by authority'
rubrics_metrics.description: The government explicitly ordered printers not to claim they were 'published by authority,' indicating a de facto freedom to print other matters and a governmental reluctance to assume supervisory responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council orders of 1725 and 1729 are cited: one prohibited printing public war affairs without government order (a constraint), while another forbade the claim of publication 'by authority' (an implicit recognition that printers might otherwise print freely except where ordered).

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and legal constraints on political reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Political items could render a publisher liable to prosecution; authorities issued orders restricting what might be printed (e.g., public affairs of war) and could pursue legal action against editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the Council's May 13, 1725 order (no printing of public war affairs without government order) and the prosecution threat against Thomas Fleet in 1742 for reporting rumors about Sir Robert Walpole. These show both explicit constraints and the practical risk to publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business and editorial practices to build circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical techniques for increasing readership and profitability—e.g., experimenting with frequency, inventing 'letters to the editor,' creating fictional characters, writing editorial paragraphs, using humor and satire—were central to a successful newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benjamin Franklin's practices are given as exemplars: beginning twice-weekly publication (later changed), originating letters-to-the-editor and editorial paragraphs, using humor (examples quoted), and publishing Poor Richard's Almanac. These are treated as deliberate circulation-building tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial patronage, partnerships, and risk-taking to found papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing and sustaining newspapers often required financial backing, partnerships, and willingness to risk capital; prominent printers aided others by funding or partnership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin's role in setting up Lewis Timothy in Charleston and partnering with other printers (e.g., James Parker) is cited to show how financial support and business arrangements were essential to spreading the press into new colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional variation in press development (North vs. South)
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth and character of the press differed regionally: the South (notably Virginia) developed journalism more slowly due to land-centered society, less urbanization, and active resistance to printing; the North and Pennsylvania forged ahead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Virginia forbade printing (no second press for forty-seven years after Buckner); Governor Berkeley's remark favoring no printing; Pennsylvania's Bradford family and the strong Whig Pennsylvania Journal; the text ties these differences to social structure (towns vs. landed proprietors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of newspapers as political mobilizers and symbolic protest
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers served as instruments of political protest and mobilization, employing symbolism, satire, and dramatic presentation (e.g., mourning issues, engravings, cartoons) to rouse public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: Pennsylvania Journal appearing in mourning with skull-and-crossbones to protest the Stamp Act; Franklin's 'Join or Die' device urging union; reprinting accounts such as the Zenger trial under headings like 'The Liberty of the Press.' These are presented as deliberate rhetorical tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing conceived as a trade transitioning to a profession with business basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Although printing was initially considered a 'trade,' figures like Franklin shifted printing and journalism onto an organized business footing, advancing professionalization of the vocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text credits Franklin with putting printing and journalism on a business basis and notes the resulting emulation (many later journalist-entrepreneurs and failures). This frames economic organization as a criterion for press sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists combining journalism with political office (journalist-statesman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners of journalism often combined editorial roles with political office or public service, thereby amplifying journalistic influence in politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benjamin Franklin's election as Clerk and later Member of the Assembly while editing his paper is given as the prototype; later figures (e.g., Horace Greeley) and the trend of journalists entering politics are noted as consequences of this combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press's role in fostering meetings, caucuses and organized political action
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers advertised, reported on, and helped organize political meetings, caucuses, and collective action (e.g., Samuel Adams' 1764 caucus), thereby aiding formal political organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Boston Evening Post's advertisements and accounts of merchant meetings and the Samuel Adams caucus are cited: the press not only reported events but actively publicized calls to organize and exert political pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language- and community-specific publishing to reach diverse populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing in languages other than English (e.g., German) and launching local papers extended the press's reach to different communities and constituencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention of attempts to print German-language papers in Germantown (1739) and Philadelphia (1743) is given as evidence that newspapers targeted linguistic communities to broaden influence and circulation.
